paper_title: GEPA-Curator: Curated Learning for Self Improving Agents

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used in multi-turn agentic workloads that require sustained interaction with complex environments. Existing reflective prompt optimizers such as GEPA learn from failed rollouts, but agentic failures can also come from prompt weaknesses, harness limitations, stochastic execution, or noisy judges. We argue that such failures may not provide useful learning signal, and may even be harmful; and thus it is essential to curate which tasks are provided to the prompt optimizer for better performance. We introduce GEPA-Curator, a framework that augments the prompt optimizer to select which agent experiences should shape prompt optimization. In particular, GEPA-Curator consists of two components: task curation, which filters out tasks that are likely to provide noisy or unreliable learning signals, and prior success retrieval, which selectively retrieves past successful trajectories for a task and provides them as additional context to the prompt optimizer. We evaluate GEPA-Curator on GoBrowse, ALFWorld, AppWorld, and $τ$-bench, using both Gemini 3.1 Pro and Claude Opus 5 as optimizer models. GEPA-Curator matches or exceeds the mean performance of both baselines, with gains of up to 20.7% over GEPA and 21.2% over ACE.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: As interest in recursive self-improvement (RSI) grows, central question is how agents can reliably learn from their own experience to improve future behavior (Favaro & Clark, 2026). Reflective prompt optimization, where an agent acts with tools in an environment and Reflector uses the resulting trajectory or end state to identify lessons and revise the agents prompt, offers one practical mechanism for this form of self-improvement (Agrawal et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026). The revised prompt is then used on subsequent tasks, creating feedback loop in which experience can progressively improve agent behavior. In agentic settings, this approach rests on the assumption that experience from previously attempted tasks contains signal and information that generalize to future tasks. However, it is often difficult for the Reflector to correctly attribute the cause of failure to the prompt. In agentic tasks, execution is mediated by harness interacting with an external environment, and success is often assessed by LLM-as-a-judge (Zheng et al., 2023). failed rollout may therefore reveal genuine prompt weakness, but it may also arise from external factors such as unavailability of needed tools, harness limitations, or even noise from execution or evaluation environments. This problem is further exacerbated in real-world settings, where tasks themselves may be ambiguous or infeasible, introducing additional noisy signals to the Reflector. When revising the prompt, the Reflector may nevertheless treat these potentially noisy observations as valid learning signals for prompt optimization (Kirichenko et al., 2025), causing it to misattribute the associated failures to prompt deficiencies, thereby producing unnecessary or harmful updates. As an example, consider an agent asked to purchase an item from shopping website. If the agent fails because it overlooks required option before adding the item to the cart, the Reflector can usefully revise the prompt to encourage checking required fields before proceeding. For example, it may conclude that the agent needs to seek alternative ways to complete the purchase, while the button can become functional for future tasks. To mitigate such issues, recent work (Agrawal et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026) uses held-out validation set in order to guard against these changes. If the prompt does poorly on the validation set after mutation, the change can be rejected. GEPA (Agrawal et al., 2026) goes step further and evaluates the mutated prompt on the minibatch again to make sure that the model performance does not degrade after such mutation. However, such validation-based gating mechanisms alone may not be sufficient to prevent noisy signals, for two reasons. First, bad mutations may be accepted and good ones rejected, e.g., because the gating decision relies on aggregated evaluation scores, which can be noisy due to stochasticity in execution or evaluation. Second, such validation-based gating acts only after mutation has been generated, and therefore cannot fundamentally improve the quality of the reflection or mutation itself. This motivates us to maintain and provide additional contextual information in order to improve the capabilities of the Reflector. Based on these insights, we present GEPA-Curator, an agentic data Curator which runs as harness on top of existing prompt optimizers. GEPA-Curator has two roles. The first is task curation, where instead of randomly selecting tasks for the minibatch, the agent will curate minibatch which is likely to provide clean signal and discard tasks which seem to be noisy or faulty. The second is prior success retrieval, where the Curator can selectively retrieve past successful trajectories for task and provide them as context to the prompt optimizer to improve the quality of the mutation. Providing the Reflector agent with successful exemplars is essential to give the model the proper context to see why the prompt is failing now, and when it succeeded in the past. Overall, our contributions are as follows: We introduce GEPA-Curator, an agentic harness for prompt optimization that improves mutation quality through adaptive task curation (Section 3.1) and selective retrieval (Section 3.2) of prior successful trajectories. We evaluate GEPA-Curator on four WebArena websites (Zhou et al., 2024), ALFWorld, AppWorld, and τ -bench. GEPA-Curator matches or exceeds the mean performance of the evaluated baselines, with gains of up to 20.7% over GEPA (Agrawal et al., 2026) and 21.2% over ACE (Zhang et al., 2026). These results suggest that the benefits of curation extend across optimizer models.

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: LLM Agents. As LLMs become ubiquitous, LLM-powered agents have been equipped with tools and harnesses in order to interact and execute in external environments. React (Yao et al., 2023) interwove reasoning with tool execution to improve performance. Later work (Patil et al., 2024; Erdogan et al., 2024; Schick et al., 2023; Shen et al., 2023; Xu et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2024) used tool calling, where the model generates structured output which is parsed and used to execute functions to affect the environment. This has led to LLM agents being used to control and interact with different environments; and this has led to variety of different benchmarks (Trivedi et al., 2024; Shridhar et al., 2021; Yao et al., 2024; Patil et al., 2024; 2025) to evaluate LLMs at tool calling. One example is using LLMs as webagents in order to explore and act in web environments (Qi et al., 2025; Erdogan et al., 2025; Gur et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2025). This has led to the development of various browser and computer use benchmarks and environments in this area (Zhou et al., 2024; Gandhi & Neubig, 2026; He et al., 2024; Xue et al., 2025; Xie et al., 2024; Yuan et al., 2026; Rawles et al., 2023). Webarena (Zhou et al., 2024) was one of the first web environments and benchmarks to cover realistic websites such as GitLab, Reddit, Shopping portals, etc. Prompt Optimization. Reflective optimizers use natural language feedback in place of numerical gradients to revise textual components of an AI system (Yuksekgonul et al., 2024; Agrawal et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026; Zhou et al., 2023b; Yang et al., 2024; Pryzant et al., 2023; Opsahl-Ong et al., 2024). In particular, GEPA (Agrawal et al., 2026) applies reflection to system-level trajectories, using evaluator feedback to diagnose failures and propose prompt mutations

ACE (Zhang et al., 2026) introduced framework for agentic context adaptation to create structured playbooks to organize and accumulate strategies at runtime. SkillOpt (Yang et al., 2026) similarly treats an agents skill document as trainable external state; separate optimizer analyzes scored rollouts and proposes bounded add, delete, or replace edits. Meta-Harness (Lee et al., 2026) extended this idea further by having an outer optimization loop on the harness code which runs the agent instead of just the prompt. These methods demonstrate that execution traces can provide substantially richer optimization signals than scalar rewards alone. GEPA-Curator addresses complementary question: which agentic trajectories provide valid signal for reflection, and what historical evidence should accompany them? Curriculum Learning. Curriculum Learning (Bengio et al., 2009; Fan et al., 2018) studies how the selection and ordering of training data can improve optimization and model training. Recent work (Zhou et al., 2023a; Chen et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024; Lee et al., 2024; Diao et al., 2024) has looked into how this can affect LLM training and alignment. LIMA (Zhou et al., 2023a) established how having poorer quality data can negatively affect LLM alignment, and showed that small amount of high-quality data can be as effective as large scale training set.

sections.title: 3 GEPA-CURATOR METHODOLOGY
sections.content: In this section, we describe how GEPA-Curator integrates with existing prompt optimizers. To do so, we first formulate prompt optimizer by its input-output interface. At each step, prompt optimizer receives prompt, minibatch of tasks, and optionally some input metadata. It executes the tasks using an actor agent conditioned on the prompt and returns an updated prompt, task-level agent trajectories, and evaluation results (See Figure 1). Ordinary prompt optimizers randomly permute and iterate through the tasks in the training dataset at each step. We identify few points in existing prompt optimizers where noisy optimization signals can arise. When selecting tasks to execute, some tasks may yield noisy or unhelpful trajectories. Furthermore, when reflecting on execution results, some failures may be difficult to attribute correctly from the failed trajectory alone. In Section 5.1, we present motivating experiments showing how such noisy signals can propagate through the optimization process and ultimately degrade training. GEPA-Curator runs as harness on top of the optimizer, maintaining per-task history, including agent trajectories and evaluation outcomes from previous optimization steps. The Curator uses this history to address these sources of noise through two corresponding roles: (i) task curation (Section 3.1), which selects tasks likely to provide useful signal for prompt optimization to construct the next minibatch; and (ii) prior success retrieval (Section 3.2), which retrieves relevant past successful trajectories for tasks in the current minibatch to provide the Reflector with concrete contextual references for failure diagnosis. Note that these trajectories are provided to the prompt optimizer only as additional input metadata, leaving the optimizer itself unchanged. The full workflow is depicted in Figure 1. We have found that both of these methods are critical for performance (Section 4.3). 3.1 TASK CURATION The Curator examines the training tasks and selects which tasks to run at each optimization step. Underexplored tasks are initially prioritized to build sufficient per-task history. As this history accumulates, the Curator may skip task when there is strong evidence that further rollouts are unlikely to yield useful reflection signal for prompt optimization. Such cases include repeated stable success, repeated failures caused by factors outside the prompt (e.g., harness or environment limitations), and inconsistent evaluations of similar outcomes, which can be judged based on the accumulated per-task history. Importantly, skipping is temporary decision rather than permanent decision, and thus skipped tasks are reconsidered by the Curator at each training epoch. This is necessary because tasks that were previously solved may regress as the prompt is updated for other tasks, e.g., through prompt compression or the addition of potentially conflicting rules. Conversely, tasks that were initially too difficult, and therefore skipped after repeated failures, may become solvable as the prompt improves and can be reintroduced into training.

sections.title: Under Review
sections.content: Figure 1: GEPA-Curator system diagram. The prompt optimizer takes in minibatch of tasks at each iteration and invokes the actor agent to execute them and performs reflective prompt optimization based on the resulting trajectories. The Curator augments the prompt optimizer by acting as an outer-loop process which traverses through the training dataset and constructs each minibatch to pass into the prompt optimizer. The Curator reads past execution trajectories for each task sampled from the training dataset and decides to run the task if doing so is likely to provide useful optimization signal (Section 3.1). The Curator can also pass prior successful trajectories for failed tasks as context to the prompt optimizer as trusted reference example (Section 3.2). Once the curated training batch of selected tasks and successful context is constructed, it is passed to the prompt optimizer for execution and optimization. The resulting trajectories and evaluation outcomes are then written back to the task history for use in subsequent curation rounds. 3.2 PRIOR SUCCESS RETRIEVAL Normally, prompt optimizers reflect on failure examples in the current minibatch and mutate the prompt based only on the failed trajectories and their evaluations. Therefore, pairing current failed execution with prior successful executions of the same task allows the Reflector to perform contrastive learning of the failed behavior against known and trusted reference. This provides the Reflector with concrete basis for correcting the behavior, rather than forcing it to diagnose the failure by guessing. The Curator is instructed to reason over the task history to select one successful trajectory that provides the most reliable reference for the current task. In particular, it favors successes supported by consistent evaluation evidence and avoids using outcomes whose apparent success is ambiguous or inconsistent with other observations in the history. When no appropriate success is available, the Curator abstains and does not provide this metadata to the Reflector. This approach prevents noisy success trajectories from providing misleading positive examples, in the same way that removing noisy failure trajectories prevents misleading optimization signals. The prompt for task curation and prior success retrieval is provided at Appendix B.2. Note that because task curation and priorsuccess retrieval are performed jointly in single Curator call, the latter requires no additional LLM invocation. In summary, these two components of GEPA-Curator (task curation and prior success retrieval) work in unison to ensure that the prompt optimizer gets cleaner and curated data to train on. By curating the tasks in each minibatch, we maximize the amount of signal provided at each step of the optimization loop through removing noisy or redundant tasks. By providing reliable past successful trajectories to the Reflector, we enable the Reflector to create better mutations with grounded understanding instead of guessing the fix.

sections.title: 4.1 EXPERIMENTAL SETUP
sections.content: We compare GEPA-Curator against GEPA (Agrawal et al., 2026) and ACE (Zhang et al., 2026). GEPA-Curator builds on simplified, greedy variant of GEPA that removes Pareto-based candidate selection. Rather than evolving candidate pool and sampling from the Pareto frontier on validation set, GEPA-Curator maintains single lineage in which each mutation becomes the next checkpoint. We evaluate the prompt every 16 iterations unless specified on held-out validation set and select the final model based on the best validation score at the end. Because our ablation showed little difference between GEPA with and without Pareto selection, we adopt this greedy variant for simplicity. The prompt-optimization experiments use gpt-oss-120b (Agarwal et al., 2025) as the actor agent. We evaluate two optimizer models, Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview (DeepMind, 2026) and Claude Opus 5 (Anthropic, 2026), using the selected model for all optimizer-side agents, including the Reflector and Curator, within each run. The minibatch size is 16. The actors maximum context length is set to gpt-oss-120Bs native maximum context length (131072) so we constrain the optimized prompt to fit within this limit. All seed prompts used for optimization are manually written. The evaluation numbers are averaged over 5 repeated runs. For evaluation of optimization on noisy data, we experimented with tasks from GoBrowse (Gandhi & Neubig, 2026): GitLab (720 tasks), Shopping (585 tasks), Shopping Admin (750 tasks), and Reddit (585 tasks) in the WebArena environment (Zhou et al., 2024). Each website is independently split 3:1:1 into train, validation, and held-out test sets. All methods use the same seed prompt, evaluator, action limits, and environment configuration. Each website/method uses 5,000 rollouts, which has been chosen to ensure that all the methods can reach their saturated success rate. We additionally evaluated on more agentic datasets, namely ALFWorld (Shridhar et al., 2021), AppWorld (Trivedi et al., 2024), and τ -bench (Yao et al., 2024). For ALFWorld, we sample 150 training tasks and 50 validation tasks from official train and valid seen splits to train with 2000 rollouts, and evaluate on all 134 valid unseen tasks. For AppWorld, we use the official dataset splits with 1500 rollouts in training, and report score based on Task Goal Completion. For τ -bench, we remove user interaction as done in (Sayana et al., 2026) by flattening all 115 interactive scenarios from the retail test set into single requests, and partition them into 48 training tasks, 32 validation, and 35 held-out test tasks with 800 rollouts. The rollout budget per benchmark was chosen to ensure that all methods can reach their saturated success rate. τ -bench specifically validates every 4 iterations due to its small training data. 4.2 MAIN RESULTS WebArena Experiments. With Gemini 3.1 Pro as the optimizer model, as shown in Table 1, GEPA improves over the seed prompt by 6.3%, whereas GEPA-Curator improves by 9.7%. GEPA-Curator improves mean held-out test success over GEPA on all four websites, with gains ranging from 1.6-7.4%. The aggregate difference between the two optimized prompts is 3.4%. Based on the displayed aggregate scores, GEPA-Curator achieves 1.54 GEPAs optimization gain over the seed. This suggests that curation materially increases how much performance can be improved from the same initial prompt. With Claude Opus 5 as the optimizer model, as shown in Table 1, GEPA improves over the seed prompt by 6.4%, whereas GEPA-Curator improves by 11.4%. GEPA-Curator improves mean held-out test success over GEPA on all four websites, with gains ranging from 0.6%-7.4%. The aggregate difference between the two optimized prompts is 5.0%. Based on the displayed aggregate scores, GEPA-Curator achieves 1.78 GEPAs optimization gain over the seed. Taken together, across both optimizer models and all WebArena domains, GEPA-Curator consistently outperforms GEPA, with aggregate improvements of 3.4% and 5.0% (and up to 7.4% for both) for Gemini 3.1 Pro and Claude Opus 5, respectively. This consistency across tasks and optimizer model choices suggests that the benefits of curation are robust rather than specific to particular run, domain or optimizer.

sections.title: 5 DISCUSSION
sections.content: 5.1 MOTIVATING EXPERIMENTS Dataset Compositions. To understand how noisy learning signals from flaky or impossible tasks can negatively impact agent learning by contaminating the prompt, we categorize GoBrowse GitLab tasks into four groups: Easy, Optimizable, Impossible, and Flaky. Easy tasks achieve constant success before optimization. Optimizable tasks initially perform suboptimally but can be improved through prompt optimization. Flaky tasks and Impossible tasks are the ones that cannot be improved, with Impossible tasks showing constant failure and Flaky tasks having mixed success due to ambiguous task intent or judge flakiness. We study how GEPA learns from Optimizable tasks under three different compositional scenarios: Optimizable + Easy, Optimizable + Impossible, and Optimizable + Flaky. Figure 2 shows the resulting learning curves. When Optimizable tasks are combined with Easy tasks, GEPA achieves near-perfect accuracy. In contrast, the accuracy only peaks at 12/16 when Optimizable tasks are mixed with Impossible or Flaky tasks. These results suggest that learning signals from Impossible and Flaky tasks can contaminate the prompt and hinder optimization. More details on how these tasks are classified and qualitative analysis of the failure cases can be found in Appendices A.1 and A.2. Numerical Curriculum Learning vs. GEPA-Curator. To test whether task selection can rely solely on binary success-failure histories, we construct dataset containing 48 Easy, 54 Optimizable, 45 Impossible, and 21 Flaky tasks. We compare against numerical curriculum learning method that adjusts task selection using only historical success and failure outcomes (detailed algorithm in Appendix A.3). As shown in Table 4, the numerical curriculum underperforms GEPA in this setting, achieving 62.5% success compared with 66.2%. In contrast, our task curation method alone achieves 67.4%, outperforming the numerical curriculum by 4.9% and GEPA by 1.2%. Most impossible-task diagnoses are attributed to harness or environment limitations, such as required tool being unavailable. These limitations also account for substantial share of flakytask diagnoses, since an actors claim that task is impossible may lead lenient judge to accept the outcome. However, ambiguous or faulty task descriptions remain the most common cause of flaky-task diagnoses. Further details are provided in Appendix C.

sections.title: 5.3 META-HARNESS-CURATOR
sections.content: Recently, Meta-Harness (Lee et al., 2026) introduced an optimization loop which acts on the harness code of agents in similar manner to how GEPA optimizes prompts. In this section, we extend the curation approach of GEPA-Curator to Meta-Harness, which we call Meta-Harness-Curator, to explore whether curation offers additional benefits when the optimizer itself has greater autonomy. Although the coding agent used in the default Meta-Harness can inspect the full execution history, it must decide which failures to investigate while also reasoning about and modifying the harness. Curation may help by directing this investigation toward focused set of tasks and relevant prior successes, providing concrete evidence to guide code changes. We hypothesize that this division of work becomes more useful as the pool of training tasks and execution histories grows. Implementation. We augment Meta-Harness with Curator that inspects candidate code, training histories, and aggregate development scores to select parent harness and subset of training tasks, together with rationale. The parent is freshly executed on these tasks, and the optimizer revises it using the resulting feedback and the Curators rationale. Each child is evaluated on the same tasks as its parent and on the full development set, regardless of whether its training score improves. Table 5 shows that adding the Curator improves Math-RAG overall test accuracy from 45.33% to 46.33% and mean reward from 45.69% to 47.26%, where reward includes partial credit for proof tasks. On text classification  (Table 6)  , overall test accuracy, averaged equally across the three datasets, increases from 48.06% to 51.04%. The gains are concentrated in LawBench and Symptom2Disease, while USPTO accuracy is slightly lower. Implementation. We introduce three modifications to improve the cost efficiency of GEPA-Curator while preserving its effectiveness: (1) Skip interval decision. Instead of making skip decision at every epoch, the Curator specifies the number of epochs to skip, eliminating repeated Curator calls during the skip interval. (2) Compact task history. Each Curator call receives full trajectories from configurable number of recent executions, while older executions are represented by compact summaries containing their epoch numbers, outcomes, and previous Curator assessments.

sections.title: 6 CONCLUSION
sections.content: In conclusion, we introduce GEPA-Curator, framework which augments prompt optimization to select which agentic tasks should shape prompt optimization. Curator is used to agentically select and filter out tasks based on whether they can provide noisy or reliable training signals. Furthermore, the Curator can retrieve and provide prior successful trajectories for failed tasks and gives them to the prompt optimizer to act as an anchoring context for reflections. We show that this technique achieves consistent performance improvements over GEPA and ACE by up to 21.2% on Webarena, ALFWorld, AppWorld, and τ -bench. We further extend our method to Meta-Harness and show that this agentic curation idea can even improve harness code as well. AI USE STATEMENT LLMs are core component of our paper. Our method uses LLMs to curate data, retrieve robust successful trajectories, and propose improvements to prompts used by an LLM agent. These LLMgenerated artifacts are part of the system being studied and developed in the paper. Furthermore, standard LLM tools were used for simple writing assistance such as grammar and formatting. ETHICS STATEMENT This work presents generic method for improving prompts for LLM agents, rather than system designed for specific domain. Potential positive impacts include making agentic systems more reliable, adaptable, and accessible to researchers and practitioners. Potential negative impacts are indirect: stronger LLM agents could be misused in harmful ways, or could cause harm if deployed in high-risk environments without proper human supervision. We emphasize that optimized agents should be evaluated in the intended environment and used with appropriate human oversight, monitoring, and controls. REPRODUCIBILITY STATEMENT The models, datasets, hyperparameters, and prompts that are used in the paper have been detailed and documented in Appendix and Section 4.1. sections.title: A DETAILS ABOUT MOTIVATING EXPERIMENTS
sections.content: A.1 SELECTION OF DATASET COMPOSITION Before constructing the experimental datasets for the motivating examples, we use logs from several preliminary GitLab experiments to identify tasks corresponding to different labels. For Easy tasks, we select tasks that already achieve consistently high success rates with the seed prompt. For Optimizable tasks, we first identify tasks that achieve consistent success with the optimized prompt from at least one preliminary GEPA run, and then select, from this subset, those with the lowest success rates under the seed prompt. For Impossible tasks, we select tasks with the lowest success rates across all rollouts. For Flaky tasks, we first identify tasks that achieve roughly 50% success with both the seed prompt and the optimized prompts returned by the preliminary GEPA runs. We then manually inspect these tasks and prioritize cases where the LLM-as-a-judge produces inconsistent success and failure judgments despite similar or identical end states, particularly when even the best attainable end state does not yield consistently successful judgments. A.2 CONCRETE EXAMPLE OF NEGATIVE TRANSFER We trace an accepted prompt mutation from iteration 7 of the Optimizable + Impossible condition. Two tasks from the Impossible partition had failed under the parent prompt. For View the split silence.py example for audio processing, global search returned no useful result, and the evaluator suggested manually browsing projects and groups. For Expand subgroup in the hierarchy list to view nested subgroups, the actor searched public groups containing no expandable subgroup, and the evaluator suggested checking the actors own groups instead. Both tasks are considered Impossible because their underspecified intents identify neither target repository nor group, leaving the actor to explore without direction, frequently exhausting its step budget before succeeding and making the tasks difficult to optimize through prompting. Reflection converted this feedback into stronger exhaustive-search instruction: Exhaustive Exploration: Global code search is often limited or disabled. If search yields no results, manually navigate through groups, projects, and repository file trees. Always check Your groups, Your projects, and your personal dashboard before defaulting to public Explore tabs, as task resources are usually associated with your account. Its exhaustive-search instruction caused regression on the Optimizable task Check the guide to WCAG documents and standards. Immediately before the mutation, the actor recognized The A11Y Project on its starting page, opened the repository, used Find file to search for WCAG, and reached src/posts/wcag2-documents.md in five actions. With the mutated prompt, instead of opening the visible A11Y Project directly, the actor first filtered its personal projects, then traversed Explore, Topics, Help, global search, and group pages. After eventually returning to the A11Y Project, it inspected the README and Wiki and manually traversed the repository tree. It exhausted all 30 actions in the src directory without reaching the guide. The exhaustive-search instruction caused the regression by replacing the short repository-level search path with broad exploration across site sections and the repository tree. Nevertheless, the aggregate minibatch score increased from 8 to 9, so the mutation was accepted as candidate 5. This example provides concrete mechanism for the trend in Figure 2: feedback from difficult tasks can elicit an overgeneralized search strategy whose aggregate gain masks regression on solvable task.

sections.title: IMPLEMENTATION OF NUMERICAL CURRICULUM
sections.content: Algorithm 1 Numerical curriculum 1: Input: task set D, b, 2: Initialize: st 0 for all 3: for each outcome (t, r) do if is failure then 4: st st + 1 5: 6: 7: 8: 9: st max(0, st k) if st > then {t} else The numerical curriculum modifies GEPAs dataset sampling procedure to progressively remove tasks that repeatedly fail during optimization. The intuition is that persistently unsuccessful tasks may contribute unhelpful feedback and cause the optimized prompt to grow unnecessarily without yielding corresponding performance gains. To identify such tasks, we maintain running score st for each task t. Whenever task fails, its score is incremented by one; when it succeeds, the score is decreased by k, lower bounded at zero. This allows occasional failures to be tolerated while assigning larger scores to tasks that fail consistently over time. Once st exceeds threshold b, the task is removed from the sampling pool for subsequent optimization iterations.

sections.title: B IMPLEMENTATION DETAILS
sections.content: B.1 MODEL DEPLOYMENT We served both openai/gpt-oss-120b and Qwen/Qwen3-8B using vLLM (Kwon et al., 2023) on single Nvidia 8H100-96GB machine for Gemini 3.1 Pro experiments and on Nvidia 4H200-141GB machine for Claude Opus 5 experiments. In both deployments, each model replica used tensor parallelism of 1, with data parallelism spanning all available GPUs (DP=8 and DP=4, respectively). Since WebArena experiments are time-sensitive, runs on the H200 node may have slight advantage due to faster actor execution from its higher memory bandwidth. This is reflected in the seed evaluation, where the Claude Opus 5 experiment achieves 0.7% higher overall score. We used temperature 1.0 for generation. The maximum sequence length was set by the model configuration: 131,072 tokens for gpt-oss-120b and 40,960 tokens for Qwen3-8B. All other vLLM settings were left at their defaults. For experiments using Gemini 3.1 Pro as the optimizer model, we used the hosted Gemini API on GCP. Gemini calls used temperature 1.0 and high thinking level. The context length, serving parallelism, and all other inference settings were left at the provider defaults. For experiments using Claude Opus 5 as the optimizer model, we used the anthropic API. Opus 5 calls used temperature 1.0, and xhigh reasoning strength.

sections.content: B.2 CURATOR PROMPTS The Curator agent in the full method makes task-selection and success-selection decisions jointly in one LLM call. For readability, we separate the shared task-selection prefix from the success-selection instructions appended when success evidence is enabled. Task-Selection Instructions You are task curator allocating evaluation budget during text optimization. Judge this task independently: no other task is visible. Decide whether another rollout is currently useful for learning better prompt or obtaining information about the task. Use these definitions: Mastered: Multiple stable, clean successes across separate rollouts. The agent must complete the task correctly, not merely benefit from evaluator luck, leaked state, or an accidentally correct final page. There must be no recent regression. One success is not sufficient evidence of mastery. Prompt-sensitive: Before/after evaluation pairs show that prompt changes can improve the behavior, including partial behavioral correction even when the binary score does not change. Run these tasks. Operationally impossible: The available tools or UI genuinely lack the required capability, supported by the action schema, trajectory-derived diagnostics, reference evaluation, or evaluator evidence. single unsupported actor claim is insufficient; repeated independent attempts consistently identifying the same missing essential capability are meaningful evidence. No current optimization signal: The same failure mode persists across multiple materially relevant prompt mutations, with no behavioral progress or new diagnostic information. Do not infer this merely because several mutations failed when they did not address the observed failure. Flaky or uninformative: Materially similar behavior and ending states repeatedly receive inconsistent outcomes without credible relationship to prompt changes. Do not infer flakiness from one disagreement. Evaluator-broken: There is explicit evidence of an incorrect label, stale or contradictory target, or an evaluator expectation inconsistent with the user request. brittle, unusually strict, or difficult evaluator is not necessarily broken. Infrastructure failure: Timeout, reset, network errors, or local-state/file collisions caused by missing resets provide no evidence about prompt quality. Do not interpret them as agent failures. Uncertain: Run rather than skip. rollout has information value: use it to test uncertain mastery, suspected flakiness, possible regressions, or ambiguous failure mechanisms. Run unseen or underexplored tasks and tasks with credible prompt-sensitive failures. Skip only when the history provides strong evidence that another rollout currently has little optimization or diagnostic value. mutation comparison records paired before/after evaluations even when the proposed mutation was rejected. Use an improved after result as evidence that the task may be prompt-sensitive, but when mutation accepted is false, do not assume that behavior belongs to the current prompt or that the task is now mastered. skip is revisited in later epoch; it is not permanent retirement. In the reason, cite the specific historical evidence supporting the decision. Select an anchor only when its behavior is genuinely correct and represents reproducible success mode, rather than an outcome caused by evaluator variance, evaluator leniency, or infrastructure variance. At least one other independent clean success must support that judgment. Use only IDs listed below and only for this task. If no success is trustworthy, use null and an empty list. skip decision must not select an anchor. Always provide separate, non-empty anchor reason. When selecting an anchor, anchor reason must explain why the selected behavior is genuinely correct and reproducible, and how the listed supporting successes corroborate it. When not selecting an anchor, anchor reason must explain why the available successes are insufficient or unsuitable. First reason about each decision, then commit to it: emit reason before decision and anchor reason before anchor success state id in the exact field order shown. Return only JSON with this exact shape: {reason:...,decision:runskip, anchor reason:...,anchor success state id:null..., supporting success ids:[]}. sections.title: C DETAILS OF CURATOR DECISIONS
sections.content: C.1 ANALYSIS OF TASK SELECTION We analyze the task-selection decisions made by the Curator across the four GoBrowse runs with Gemini 3.1 pro as optimizer. Table 9 reports tasks that the Curator explicitly described as impossible or flaky (and thus were not selected for the corresponding training batch) at any point during optimization. The two diagnosis categories overlap for 8 tasks: 18 impossible and 65 flaky diagnoses cover 75 unique tasks in total. We further manually classify each impossible diagnosis according to its primary cause. As shown in Table 10, most impossible diagnoses arise from limitations of the execution harness or deployed environment, such as missing feature, unavailable state, or unsupported action. Faulty tasks instead omit necessary information, impose an infeasible scope, or otherwise fail to specify satisfiable objective. We separately retain speculative diagnoses and diagnoses later overturned by additional evidence. We apply the same cause analysis to the 65 tasks that the Curator described as having flaky evaluation. Table 11 shows that faulty or underspecified tasks constitute the largest group, followed by harness or environment limitations, which can lead judges to accept an actors claim that it cannot complete the task. We also identify four tasks with reliable, reproducible success behavior for which the evaluator occasionally produced false negatives by applying harsher or shifting criteria.

Open streaks and reruns in partial final epochs are excluded. Taken together, these analyses suggest that GEPA-Curator can identify tasks whose outcomes are unlikely to provide reliable optimization signals. Many of the tasks diagnosed as impossible or flaky are affected by inherent limitations of the execution harness or environment, or by faulty or underspecified task descriptions. By withholding these tasks from the corresponding training batches, GEPA-Curator prevents their potentially misleading outcomes from influencing those optimization steps. Importantly, an impossible or flaky diagnosis does not permanently retire task. The diagnosis may be uncertain, and subsequent prompt updates or further actor exploration may reveal that task previously considered impossible is solvable. The Curator therefore reconsiders skipped tasks in subsequent epochs. To analyze this behavior, we divide the complete training epochs into three phases and measure the consecutive skipped epochs preceding each rerun. As shown in Table 12, impossible tasks are deferred the longest, with their mean skip streak increasing from 5.50 to 8.75 epochs. Mastered tasks are also deferred longer over time because repeated stable successes reduce the expected value of additional rollouts, although they are periodically revisited to detect regressions. Flaky tasks are revisited more frequently to resolve uncertainty. Thus, curation adjusts task frequency rather than permanently excluding tasks. Furthermore, skip streaks generally increase as task histories accumulate, making the Curator more confident that rerunning task at the current stage is unlikely to provide new information for prompt optimization. While the Curator diagnosed 75 of the 1,581 training tasks (4.7%) as impossible or flaky at least once during optimization, its effect on optimization is non-trivial. Under uniform minibatch sampling, as in GEPA, minibatch of 16 tasks contains at least one such task with probability 1 (1 0.047)16 54%. Moreover, reflection is driven by failures, and these tasks fail far more often than the rest of the training set, assuming impossible tasks fail consistently and flaky tasks roughly half the time. As Appendix A.2 illustrates, even one or two such failures can elicit an overgeneralized mutation that passes minibatch gating while regressing solvable task. C.2 ANALYSIS OF SUCCESS SELECTION As optimization progresses, successful trajectories accumulate and become available as reflection anchors (see Table 13). The proportion of failed reflection instances paired with retrieved successful trajectory increases from 6.9% in the early phase to approximately 50% in the middle and late phases. Early failures are predominantly unpaired because no historical success exists (75.5%), whereas among late failures, 31.1% still have no historical success and 18.6% have an available success pool but receive no anchor because the Curator abstains. We analyze success-state selection over the 554 unique tasks for which failed rollout entered reflection while at least one historical success state was already available (see Table 14). selection is considered relevant when, at the time of selection, the history contains both reliable success state and at least one noisy success state (e.g. evaluator leniency, contaminated environment state) and the Curator selects the reliable state. We identify 17 such tasks (3.1%). We separately count meaningful abstention: cases in which the historical success pool is non-empty, but the Curator selects no anchor because it explicitly identifies the available score-positive states as untrustworthy, contradictory, state-contaminated, evaluator-lenient, or unsupported by consistent reproducible success mode. We exclude abstentions caused only by Curator-output validation failure, as well as generic cases where single success merely lacked second corroborating rollout. Under this conservative definition, meaningful abstention occurs for 50 tasks (9.0%).
